subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is the first time I have had the chance to speak since the session started, may I first of all heartily congratulate the Speaker who will chair this session's debates and, hopefully, several future debates as well.
I wish to assure him that he will enjoy our wholehearted co-operation. The experience which I have gleaned through a few years in the House has led me to understand that the Speaker, despite all his qualities, needs the cooperation of all hon. members in order to discharge his fairly onerous duty and chair the debates for the good not only of the members, but also of all Canadians, whose representatives we are here, so that the debates can be led to their anticipated results.
Mr. Speaker, we are today starting to study a bill providing for the settlement of a strike which has been going on for several weeks on the west coast. The examination of this bill does not occur in a traditional setting. We had to adjourn the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne to face a situation which has suddenly become serious. This strike has been going on for several weeks, as I stated earlier. Early in August, the Social Credit Party of Canada asked the government to resume parliamentary work in order to bring about an end to this trike, since we had foreseen that it would be a lengthy one. Our experience of previous conflicts led us to doubt that this strike could be settled without the government being forced to resort to legislation.
However, Mr. Speaker, the government turned a deaf ear to our claims and we were not alone in this. The other parties as well as farm and trade organizations throughout Canada called for government action.
The minister just told us a moment ago that the Governor-in-Council, at the outset of the election campaign, suspended the right to strike in this Pacific port until election day because it would apparently have been detrimental to the Canadian economy. But a few weeks too late, it is realized that the government did not fear as much for the Canadian economy as for the economy of the
Grain Handlers' Strike
Liberal party, because if a strike could affect the Canadian economy during the election campaign, its effect would be the same after the election. Still, the government waited three months before acting to put an end to this strike.
Mr. Speaker, we are aware that this method of settling a labour conflict is not too popular either with trade unions or with employers.
Given the context, this procedure is becoming popular with Canadians. And we know that a strike of such magnitude has a high cost to the nation's economy and everyone loses. Grain handlers in western ports are the first victims of the strike, but employers also lose. Grain producers, especially those in the Prairies, stand to lose much from the strike. Canadian trade also loses a great deal. On this point, I do not expect our overseas clients to be happy with those ever repeating strikes.
On August 31, 1972, a special session was called to settle a strike in western ports, quite similar to the one before us today. On August 30, 1973, almost a year to the day, a special session was called to settle a Canadian railroad strike, following an earlier one. On October 7, 1974, a special bill was passed to settle a strike in western ports, and in October 1975 we will probably be debating a bill to settle a labour dispute in some federal area, probably a harbour strike, maybe an eastern one this time involving the Atlantic or the St. Lawrence. It may be a mail strike, or a railroad or an air transport strike.
The same situation will probably occur next year.
Mr. Speaker, what are the provisions in the bill before us to settle the strike? Upon passage of the bill, the workers will be forced to go back to work. The strikers will have to return to work, the companies that imposed the lockout will have to call workers back on the job. The employees are told: You will get 87 cents more an hour starting December 1, 1973. An arbitrator is appointed to help settle the dispute, to find points of agreement, to negotiate a labour contract for the next few months.
But then, Mr. Speaker, if it is possible to appoint an arbitrator today in an attempt to solve the dispute, why could it not be done two months ago for instance to end this conflict which has caused so many problems at all levels of the Canadian economy? We waited until today. Mr. Speaker, a question still remains; probably tomorrow morning, or as soon as the bill is passed, the worker will be forced back to work, with an offer of 87 cents an hour. But how much will he get out of that increase of 87 cents an hour?
Part of this 87 cents will go to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) who will hand it to the government of British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, I expect the government to take in taxes 30 to 40 per cent of that increase which the companies will be forced to pay their employees. The worker will come out of that strike a loser because management will have to raise its freight rates and profits to meet the higher wages they will have to pay. But the worker, the grain handler who will be forced back to work tomorrow morning will receive only part of that increase.
He will get only part of that increase, and come out a loser. Mr. Speaker, it is the same thing at all levels,

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
whether it be in the public or the private sector in Canada. There is always a salary increase following a labour dispute. But every time the government takes its share of the increase, so the worker is always a loser. He always wants to boost his purchasing power but he is worse off than before.
Mr. Speaker, what the Canadian worker wants, be it in the field of production or public services, Pacific or Atlantic ports, transportation or private enterprise, is first and foremost a purchasing power high enough to allow him to meet his own needs and those of his family. That is what the worker is seeking, Mr. Speaker, and today that possibility is taken away from him on account of the price rise which is practically accepted and which seems to be encouraged because it suits the government. In the production field for instance, every wage increase means a price increase. Therefore, the government is taking not only a part of that increase through income tax, but it also increases its revenues indirectly through an increase in the federal tax and in the provincial sales tax. Therefore, the government wins on all counts.
That is why the worker is ever more deprived of the fruit of his work and is endeavouring by all means to strengthen his purchasing power. The only thing he can do at the present time, is to call for higher wages.
Mr. Speaker, such a situation cannot last any longer. If an effective way of putting an end to it is not found rapidly, there will never be any way out and we will get bogged down deep.
The bill before us will not solve anything. It will force workers, grain handlers in the Pacific ports to go back to work, but afterwards, we will have to start afresh.
We had a debate on August 31, 1972, during which the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), said the following, which I am quoting from page 3910 from the official report of the House of Commons Debates:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-231 is not the solution to the problem. We know we will have to begin all over again, for the same causes generally produce the same results.
The leader of the Social Credit Party said that two years ago. We now face exactly the same problem in the same area.
Mr. Speaker, we must find other means to solve this problem, to avoid Parliament-having to deal with such conflicts time and time again. The Social Credit Party of Canada has often asked that a labour court be established, not to settle labour disputes, but to prevent them. This is what the leader of our party asked once again that same day in the same speech. He said, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that a Canadian labour court be created as soon as possible in order to prevent disputes and to maintain the best possible relations between labour and management.
Mr. Speaker, this suggestion should be accepted and recognized by the government. It is up to the government to decide whether to institute such a labour court, as I said, and as was said often before, not to settle labour conflicts, but mostly to prevent them.
Mr. Speaker, this will obviously not be sufficient if the government does not take the necessary means, not only to stop the present increase in the cost of living, but also to

reduce it so that the Canadian dollar may regain its former value. In this way, the Canadian worker who lives on a pension or a fixed income, who has saved some money, will not lose the value of his dollar. Mr. Speaker, I believe that the government has the duty to control inflation, and that this should be done even before the institution of a labour court.
Mr. Speaker, those are two important subjects with which the government should deal immediately. It must do so during this session if it wants to act seriously and be taken seriously by the Canadian voters. Everyone suffers from the situation, and there is no saying that our overseas clients may not tire at some point or other, whether it be in connection with grain or other goods we offer them, of seeing those delays occur at every turn and look to other producers, to other exporting countries. There again, we would suffer from not being able to export our surpluses.
Mr. Speaker, that is the message I wanted to contribute to the debate on this bill. As for me, I feel it should be passed as soon as possible, to put an end to a conflict which has lasted much too long; we should also take the necessary steps, during this session, to ensure that this situation does not constantly recur in the future as it has especially in the last few years.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not without a considerable degree of trepidation that I, as a freshman member of this House, rise to make my first remarks in this chamber in the course of this crucial debate with respect to the west coast grain handlers' dispute.
As the representative of Assiniboia constituency-one of this nation's greatest agricultural and, particularly, grain producing regions-this dispute and its settlement are of paramount concern to me at the moment. It is essential that the interruption in Vancouver grain movement be brought now to a speedy conclusion by parliament because it is quite apparent that exhaustive efforts- they have been exhaustive on all sides-toward a negotiated solution have not been, and will not be, successful.
I regret-as I am sure most hon. members of this House regret-the fact that we are here today dealing with this problem in this manner. Surely the floor of this House must not become the commonplace location for major labour-management negotiations in this country to take place. The prime responsibility in this area, through the collective bargaining process, rests-and ought to rest- with employers and employees. Under our laws, and in the national interest in most cases, they are quite properly called upon to sit down together to resolve their differences, find common ground and reach contract settlements without damaging slowdowns or destructive work stoppages, and without possible mischief or violence and the eventual necessity of parliamentary intervention. But in the present circumstances, parliament has no alternative but to take this action, and I hope expeditiously, to conclude a contract so that our grain exports through Vancouver can resume.
October 7, 1974

I must say that I appreciate the view expressed by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party, that his party wants this legislation to move forward quickly so that grain can begin to move through Vancouver. I regret the attitude of the official opposition, which seems not to be very concerned about the situation at the moment.
I suppose somewhere in the annals of our industrial history we might find what could be described as examples of perfect negotiations or perfect industrial relations. But most surely these examples would be few and far between in our less than perfect world. The present situation in Vancouver falls far short of perfection when viewed from almost any perspective, and the difficulties of this past summer have taken place against a sorry background of sour relationships and discord extending back more than a decade. In view of this sad history, I particularly welcome the proposal today by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) that an industrial inquiry commission will soon be appointed to thoroughly investigate the history of labour relations in the grain handling industry at Vancouver.
Requests for such a move have come from such diverse sources as the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association and, I believe, the National Farmers' Union. I know we will all wish the commission well in its work toward achieving a better industrial relationship between the grain handling companies and their employees. I am sure prairie grain producers are looking forward to an era of more stability in this field so that they need not fear further costly disruptions in the movement of their grain into export position.
There are two general issues with which I shall deal briefly. First, some parties in this House and outside have tried to paint the government as the ogre in this sad situation. I ask members, before they make their judgment in this case, to look carefully at the chronology of events which stretch back for one year. Negotiations began for a new contract on October 19, 1973, almost a full year ago. The existing contract was due to expire on November 30. Direct negotiations between the parties continued for almost two months, without success.
The parties requested federal mediation assistance about the middle of December, 1973. That assistance was forthcoming immediately and two skilled mediators struggled to find reasonable common ground for agreement between the parties. They worked for another two months but were unable to show signs of progress. A clear impasse had been reached and the Minister of Labour moved to appoint as conciliation commissioner Dr. Perry, who began his duties on February 15, 1974, four full months after discussions had begun originally. So this was hardly a premature move.
The appointment apparently was well received. Dr. Perry is a skilled man, an expert who is widely respected and well known in the field and, as the minister pointed out earlier, he had worked with these same parties a few years previously. It is interesting to note that amid all the controversy surrounding the dispute nobody has attacked Dr. Perry's competence, ability or impartiality. There has been criticism from some sides of the recommendations he
Grain Handlers' Strike
put forward, yet nobody has attacked his ability to deal with the situation or his competence in the field. Dr. Perry worked with both sides for 214 months but was unable to draw them together. Finally, he produced a report recommending what he saw to be a fair and reasonable settlement.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Surely it was a basis for settlement.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, it was a basis for settlement. Those words are important. This was the best advice available to the parties and to the government of Canada. Clearly, he had done a sound and thorough job in the circumstances. The Perry report in itself was the end product of this particular collective bargaining process. We must keep that point in mind. It was a process which the parties themselves over a period of 614 months, with all the help in the world, had failed to make work.
What was the government to do with Dr. Perry's report? Could it reasonably, after all that had gone before, say, "No, we don't particularly care for this report. We will put it aside and appoint another conciliation commissioner who will work with the parties for another 2 Vi months and produce another report which we may or may not accept?" And on and on the process could go.
Clearly, once the parties directly involved in the negotiations, the employers and employees, had allowed their negotiations to deteriorate over more than half a year to the point where an expert, impartial third party had to investigate the situation and produce a thorough report, with recommendations, all the parties, the employers, employees as well as the government, had to be prepared to give that particular report some credence, authority and weight. The view adopted by the government was that the Perry report could not simply be tossed aside as unworthy of discussion.
The government urged this view on all sides, privately and eventually publicly. The workers agreed to it, the companies did not. To ensure continued grain movement during the period parliament was in dissolution, the government acted under section 181 of the Canada Labour Code to prevent a strike or lock-out, indeed to prevent a stoppage in grain exports, until August 8. All the while efforts continued at the official and ministerial level to have negotiations resume on the basis proposed by Dr. Perry. His report was clearly intended to be a basis for further negotiation, but this negotiation did not prove successful. Finally, in late August all work stopped. Exhaustive efforts to bring about a voluntary settlement failed. Further efforts would be pointless. And here we are today.
Allegations of blame are not helpful if we are to reach lasting solutions to difficult problems of this nature, but I believe two points should be put on record. First, once it was made clear to the representatives of the union that the government, if forced to do so, would legislate an end to the dispute on the basis of principles contained in Dr. Perry's report-again, these words were carefully chosen-there could be no excuse for continuing a work slowdown which hampered grain movement. That course of action was not responsible, and perhaps contributed to the further deterioration in relations. It certainly added to the harm done to western grain producers.

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
Second, once it was made clear to the companies that the government, if forced so to do, would legislate on the basis of Dr. Perry's principles-again, these are important words-it was illogical for them to persist in refusing to discuss the report and work out a settlement on the basis of the report. The final result, as we are witnessing today, was clearly inevitable. The companies said they were standing on principle in demanding parliamentary action. But it should be borne in mind that that standing on principle resulted in substantial losses being borne by prairie producers. They are losses which could have been avoided if the companies had accepted voluntarily, several weeks ago, the result which they then knew would be inevitable. If they had wanted to avoid responsibility, if they had wanted a scapegoat, they could have pointed the finger at the government. In the meantime they could have saved western farmers several million dollars.
It is interesting to consider the figures to which the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) referred.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: The grain companies do not pay demurrage; the Wheat Board does.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Demurrage charges totalling nearly $10 million have been incurred over the past several weeks, because grain has not been moving. As I said, it is interesting to note the figures mentioned by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. For instance, the total cost of the increases suggested by the Perry report might be $3.5 million, perhaps $4 million, over two years. The demurrage charges alone which the Wheat Board has had to pay would have paid 2 Vi times for the increases in the new contract.
Given this recent chronology of events, the long history of sour labour relations in this industry on the west coast and the difficult attitudes adopted at times by both sides, and given the work done by Dr. Perry in his 2 Vi months of effort, the government's action in the circumstances has been fair and reasonable. Let me point out-this is particularly important to grain producers-that if the government had pursued a course of action other than the one it did, we probably would have seen a full work stoppage, perhaps a violent one, not in late August but perhaps in May, in April or even earlier. The grain kept moving, albeit at a slower rate, until the last week of August. That, in itself, was a considerable contribution in view of what might have happened.
Let me say one final word about the figures. Percentages have been mentioned in this House, in the press and elsewhere. Anyone who wants to put forward a view can sharpen his pencil and come forward with calculations in its support. When you break it down, Dr. Perry in his recommendations makes three separate points. They must be separated, because if you try to add them together you are adding apples and oranges. He talks about wages, about a cost of living adjustment and about a pension plan. If you break down the wage figures, you will see clearly that the increases range from 31 per cent to 32 per cent over two years, which is 15 per cent of 16 per cent per year. In terms of the situation in Vancouver, perhaps even the national situation, that would not be out of line when you are talking about a wage package exclusive of a cost of living adjustment.

When considering the pension plan provisions, bear in mind there had not been, by and large, any effective plan in place for the past several years for these particular employees at Vancouver. Clearly, the pension plan figures cannot be simply lumped in with the wage figures. There is a qualitative difference between an increase and having a pension plan at all. They cannot simply be added together to come up with some grotesque figure which does not fairly reflect the situation.
I do not want to take up any further time of the House dealing with the arguments pro and con the particular politics of the situation. As we go about our difficult task today, the problems are serious enough. I hope there will be a speedy resolution. None of us like the job we are called upon to do today, but I urge the House to pass expeditiously the legislation before us so that the crucial product, the grain, can begin to move. As this serious dispute ends, as the employees go back to work and the grain moves into export position, I hope all members of this House and all Canadians will heighten our resolve to find in the long run a better way.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue we are discussing today is like a gramaphone record I have been hearing for 20 years; the more things seem to change on the west coast, the more they remain the same.
I wish to congratulate the new member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) for presenting the government case so logically. I congratulate him on his delivery. However, I must warn him that he will never succeed in being a lasting success in this House by becoming an apologist for those "two babes in blunderland" who wandered around on this issue this past spring.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
There is a mess on the west coast and everyone knows it. These stoppages we have had since 1965 are going to continue this fall, next spring, and forever after. If it is not the grain handlers, it will be the longshoremen or some other group. All I can say is that the job to which we should be addressing ourselves is how we are going to eliminate these perennial stoppages. All parties agree that is our job. I wish to direct my attention to what are the issues.
First, there is a gulf or gap between labour men and management that is too wide to bridge by the absolute and sterile methods now being used in labour-management negotiations. The rigidity and barrenness of this approach are not only hitting Canadian producers of grain, but hitting the world in a way the continuation of which we cannot tolerate. I am referring to the fact that there is a hungry world out there.
These working men and farmers know as well as I that we have a job to do. We know what stands in our way is this barren, sterile labour-management type of procedure that is laid down. It is not for me to lay down a new labour-management procedure. I just want the House to know that the misinformation given to us by the hon. member for Assiniboia is very simple. He talked about two months and four months of exhaustive negotiations. I can
October 7, 1974

assure this House that both management and labour agree on one thing. There were no real negotiations at any time. That is the first point.
I am not here to kick the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) around. I have more important things to do at this time. In passing over the events, I believe that management blundered badly. Because of its impatience it brought in this government machinery last fall and put itself on a slippery slope it could not get off.
I do not blame management for being annoyed when no negotiations took place. Suggestions for negotiations were put before them in the Perry report. The government stepped in and in effect said, "Even if there are no negotiations, we will legislate this proposal into being". By all the evidence on both sides, there was infringement of the legalistic type of labour-management negotiations which are set up under the government machinery. There is no debate on either side of the issue on that score.
All this talk and hammering at each other does not get at the question of stopping the grain stoppages. We must be aware, as we should have been aware for the past 25 or 30 years, that the food crisis is coming upon us in increasing crescendos. We have to do our part. The producers and working men both know this.
As pointed out by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), the farmers want to move grain. They know that for years we moved grain through terminals on the west coast for a reasonable amount. We kept it at six cents a bushel because increasing costs were met by growing productivity.
Some of us from the PC caucus went to the west as a group of people, not to negotiate or interfere, but to determine facts. We found that what the Perry report and what various government officers in the negotiations talked about are altogether different from what labour wanted to talk about. Labour wanted to talk about how they could increase efficiency, productivity and get incentives for this new type of work force people they have to deal with, the young men. They wanted better communications with their boss.
As everyone knows, the bulk of the grain going through the west coast is put through terminals owned by co-operatives which have their headquarters on the prairies. These democratically owned co-operatives delegate to local management the running of these terminals. When they deal with the 550 men in this local, they do not deal with them as human beings. They hire the best lawyer that money can buy; $500 a day. To earn that pay, he is going to grind down on every point that he can.
We hear about the dirty tricks division of the politicians. You should see the dirty tricks division in this type of negotiation. I do not blame the lawyer for doing the best job he can to make the best deal possible for management. That is his job. However, this is not a sterile, barren situation where you are dealing with automation.
The young men in the labour force in that part of the country are the same as your sons or mine. They are 25 or 30 years of age. To them dollars and cents are not the only issue. They want to know why they have to work in that dusty, dirty environment, why there is only one toilet for
Grain Handlers' Strike
130 men, and why there are no shower facilities in some of these places. They want to know why they have these working conditions that most of us do not have to endure. They will put up with this if they know why.
These are modern-day human problems. Since labour wish to talk about efficiency and incentives or, as they call it, better communications, I think if would be easy to formulate a program of action. The bill before us does nothing to settle the basic grievances which have arisen on both sides, between two sincere groups of people, over the last 20 years.
The minister tells us he will appoint an industrial inquiry commission. I do not care how many he appoints. Any farmer I know, with half the brains he was born with, could sit down with his opposite number in this labour union, also with half the brains he was born with, and come up with a solution within two or three days without fooling around with an inquiry or anything else.
I realize the whole labour-management situation in the industry is in a mess and needs inquiry. But in this particular job, faced as we are with the challenge to keep grain moving, the first step in any action program should be to see to it that the presidents of these co-operatives and privately-owned terminals out there meet face to face with their opposite numbers in this little labour union. Let one of the terms of reference relate to ways of increasing productivity and, believe me, if these men do as they have done before, they will give us this increased productivity, and there will be no inflation at all.
Any agreement which raises wages even by 5 per cent is inflationary if there is no corresponding increase in productivity. But if these men, as they have done before-and thank God for it-increase their productivity, there should be no unwillingness to pay them more automatically without the silly farce of a strike. Therefore, as part of this action program, we need those directly affected-the leaders of the farm organizations, the employers and the heads of the labour unions-to meet in an effort to produce this new type of contract which includes productivity formulae and the provision of incentives, and to agree that grain, a food absolutely necessary in the world today, should be taken out of the field of labour-management disputes.
There is enough of an Irishman in each of us that we like a fight now and then, but these disputes should not result in the stoppage of vital food exports. I believe the longshoremen would also agree. I submit that the Perry report does not meet the criteria I have outlined. I have read it a number of times but I found no mention of productivity, no mention of increased efficiency, no mention of incentives for these men so that they would want to work-

That is right. It was not in the terms of reference. That is what happens once one begins to think in legal terms and put these matters in the hands of lawyers. We should never forget that we are dealing here with human beings. My point is simple.

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
I do not care how fine the Perry report may be or how bad it may be. It does not meet the basic criteria which must be met in the interests of the farmers and the workers. It does not deal with the need for increased productivity or increased efficiency, possibly brought about by increased automation and so on. For this reason it does not deal with the root problem. And because it does not deal with these things it is inflationary. The employees do not want a settlement to be inflationary. They want to accept the principles of productivity, of efficiency, of incentives and, above all, of improved communications with management. If, by these means, they can move more bushels of grain through the port, there is no inflation involved.
In many industries it is hard to quantify gains in productivity or efficiency. But that is not true of the grain business. The number of bushels or carloads moved in a year, a month, a day or an hour can be precisely measured. If the men's ideas can lead to increased productivity I know the farmer will wish the workers get their reward for producing those ideas and putting them into practice. Similarly, if it is machinery or new technology which leads to increased productivity, management has the right to share in the gains as well.
I think it can be gathered I am speaking with some feeling on this subject because I had to endure some anxious times myself in 1961. After a decade in which the farmers had been completely up against it, we finally found a little market for 60 million bushels a year in China. And my experts in the department, in the Wheat Board, on the Board of Grain Commissioners, the Harbour Commission, and management out there, told me with great sincerity and conviction that it was impossible to move that amount of grain via the west coast. Well, Mr. Speaker, when one has fought so hard to achieve something it is awful to be told by the experts that you cannot do it.
I know nothing about moving grain, but I do know something about human beings. I asked the railway heads and the farm representatives and the labour representatives-17 different groups in all-to meet to consider this challenge. And, believe me, in five days those human beings doubled the productivity of those port facilities without a dollar being spent in new capital investment. Nearly all the ideas came from the labour side. The increased flow dramatically increased the gross income of the companies, and when I suggested that labour surely deserved some of it, management said, "Very well, 10 per cent will go to labour." This represented a 60 per cent increase, yet not one voice was raised in complaint, because productivity had been doubled. I am talking now about the basic wage.
When we added up the extra $1.5 million which went to them it meant an increase of 60 per cent in their basic rate. Workers came to me at that time and said, "We have worked for this company for 20 years but this is the first time we have met our boss, and he is not such a bad fellow after all". They gave their word that as long as the oral agreement then reached was in being there would never be a strike by grain handlers or longshoremen on the west coast.

That was the situation until the companies made the mistake, in 1965, of hiring a lawyer who introduced a side issue of one kind or another. As a result, there was a breakdown. The companies, realizing their mistake, got rid of that lawyer and hired another. This brings me back to square one.
I think I should conclude, Mr. Speaker, by putting my arguments in point form. I should like to suggest that when the presidents of these grain companies sit down with their opposite numbers in the labour union they immediately agree, as they agreed in 1961, that we need a single grain allocation authority. Whether or not this be a transportation man, we need a grain allocation authority, someone who can direct the traffic and stop this silly sort of thing that is taking place in the name of competition.
Secondly, I suggest they accept the fact that we need a new grain handling system on the prairies to tie up with the modernization of the grain handling system on the coast. This has been held up for 25 years, for reasons that only people on the prairies understand.
Thirdly, I suggest they should discuss with the co-ops, and then recommend to the government, a new tax system that allows equality of tax treatment for private enterprise which is competing with the co-ops both on the prairies and in the terminals. That is the only way to protect the interests of both farmer and workers.
Fourthly, to get the grain moving and keep it moving, they should immediately accept the concept of a 24 hour a day operation in all the terminals, seven days a week, and put an end to the two shifts a day, five days a week pattern. They should work with the railways instead of against the railways.
I happen to know that there will be a volume of products coming through to the west coast greater than management knows about, certainly greater than even the labour fellows expect. These products that will be coming from the prairies in the next two decades are going to require tremendous efficiency in handling capacity on the west coast.
I should like to repeat that nothing is new, as I said in my opening remarks. But I felt keenly enough about this six years ago to propose a type of contract that now I hope labour and the company presidents will consider. These proposals were put forward in 1968, not in 1974, and are quite simple.
First, there should be a cost of living clause, and secondly, an agreed upon productivity gain rate, which gain would be shared on a formula mutually arrived at between management and labour. Thirdly, there should be constant negotiation to allow for external influences and new information. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, these words have meaning both to labour and to management. Fourthly, there should be provided built-in inducements to maximize productivity, and fifthly, participation of both sides in a program of labour supply, training, etc. Lastly, I would add a grievance procedure that could be activated continually and quickly. I suggest such a grievance procedure is obviously required. When men work under difficult and dirty conditions a fight soon develops, and it is better to
October 7, 1974

Grain Handlers' Strike
settle it within 24 or 48 hours than let it turn into a great sore.
I have taken my full time, Mr. Speaker, but I plead with the House, as I have on many previous occasions. We know that the Perry report is going to go through, and you cannot blame labour for accepting it. On the other hand, you cannot blame management for screaming its head off at the way things were handled. Nevertheless the real issue is to get at the basic problems on the west coast. Perhaps when we get all straightened around, since the system is more efficient by far on the west coast than on the east coast, we can then start work on the system on the east coast and bring about the same efficiency there.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate you on your election and assure you of my full and entire co-operation in the carrying out of your duties which I hope will last for a long time. I also wish to offer you my services if necessary.
Mr. Speaker, in the discussion of the bill entitled: "An Act to provide for the resumption of grain handling operations on the west coast of Canada" we have to deal with the basis of negotiations for collective agreements and to show more especially how a conflict can deteriorate at the social and humanitarian levels. That kind of conflict can give rise to a crisis which can sometimes be called a national crisis, because those individuals must work to ship abroad the grain necessary for the survival of people. Those workers have to earn reasonable wages for their work.
My hon. colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain made quite relevant remarks on the negotiation. He pointed out the need for continued negotiation in collective agreements. I would agree with him because I participated for seven or eight years in negotiations coming up every two or three years. One could see that those negotiations kept coming back on the same technical details. They were negotiated, and there was indeed a considerable loss of time. On the other hand, to have on-going negotiation, those parties would indeed have to act in good faith, and show respect one for the other.
I think that in this conflict management showed no respect at all for its employees. On the contrary, they refused to play their economic role by refusing to discuss negotiable demands and saying that Dr. Perry's recommendations were similar to those made in 1970. I do not consider Dr. Perry's recommendations to be so extravagant because in the province of Quebec about 100,000 workers in the public or quasi-public service now have that. If the expected rise in the cost of living is set at about 4 per cent and actually turns out to be 7 per cent I do not see anything abnormal in saying that the difference between 4 and 7 per cent is 3 per cent. This is a fair increase that the government of Quebec gives all its employees.
I think the recommendations contained in the report are a decent minimum for those employees, a minimum that will merely allow them to catch up on the dock workers who work with them everyday. I think that should be considered as a minimum that is certainly not extravagant and will not contribute to fuel inflation. I, for one, do not think that inflation is the result of salary increases. Many other factors cause inflation. When there is talk of productivity, of yield, no mention is made of the high cost of money, of the rate some people charge: there is a marked preference for talking about the rate of production of the human being.
To my mind, claiming that granting an increase to those people will cause inflation is trying to evade the problem.

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
I should also like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) for the way in which he dealt with the problem. First of all, I firmly believe that he gave the two parties a chance to come to an agreement before asking Parliament to intervene. Let us go back to the beginning of the conflict. It will be recalled that in September of 1973, more specifically on September 17, 1973, the unions advised the company of their wish to negotiate. Here we are in October 1974 and negotiations between the two parties have been a complete failure. Why? For several reasons, and I believe the preamble to Dr. Perry's report should be quoted to understand precisely what the merits of the claims and why it was impossible to reach an agreement based on compromise before being forced to pass an act of Parliament.
Dr. Perry said in part that the effects of the rising cost of living, especially in the second year of the old collective agreements, gave the workers a distinct feeling of being cheated and a sound conviction that the loss in purchasing power should be made up one way or another.
Widely spread uncertainties as to the future trend of consumer prices had stirred up fears with respect to the validity of a long term contract at this time.
There were other important considerations. For example, there was no pension plan for the whole industry on the west coast. A pension plan without contributions was being established; there were also frequent cases of higher wage scales in related industries, clear differences in the hopes of both parties regarding what could be achieved in that year through amendments. Furthermore, the negotiations were made difficult by previous negotiations.
In such circumstances, the subsequent recommendations could only indicate a series of provisional changes which both parties could accept while trying to reach an agreement in such a difficult year.
I think that in the previous conflict between the companies and the employees lies the explanation for the sad state of these negotiations.
There are probably some difficulties with the union, but most of all there is bad faith towards the western coast employers.
A quick look at the recommendations Dr. Perry made is enough to make one wonder why the parties did not agree.
First, as far as money is concerned, the people are asking for a 15 per cent increase that Dr. Perry supports. And we learned from the minister that the annual pay rise in British Columbia last year was 15.7 per cent. Therefore, I do not think that Dr. Perry was overly generous in making this recommendation.
Second, to contend, in 1974, that there must be a two year contract is to me quite normal. That was another rejected recommendation.
Third, he said there will be a further general increase of 65 cents as of December 1, 1974.
Fourth, he referred to cost of living adjustments to hike any increase of more than 4 per cent a year.
At the outset I explained that this practice is frequent, at least in Quebec, in the civil service and related bodies since 1970. I can't imagine why workers on the waterfront could not be granted similar benefits, whether they are

employed by government or private enterprise. If private enterprise really wants to show leadership and demonstrate that it has a social part to play in Canada, it is in cases such as this one that it should do so. If they are not of good faith and force us to sit today, then these companies compel us once more to settle problems they brought on themselves. What employer today would dare refuse to grant a pension plan? It is indeed impossible to understand that such employers still exist. Most of the changes proposed by Dr. Perry are minor changes in the area of employer-employee relations. Indeed they are far from being major changes.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know where we could go if we had such firms everywhere in Canada. First of all, our time would be spent intervening between unions and employers, something I should greatly deplore. In my opinion, the settlement of a conflict ought to be left to the parties involved.
This is a very special situation. For the past year and a half, the government has been at least trying to appoint a special investigator to help settle the problem between the parties, and it is realized, after reading the report, that there was always one party which refused to accept Dr. Perry's recommendations.
The management knew that it just did not have to accept. To wash its hands of the matter, it knew that someday a responsible government like ours would take means to solve the problem, and that once we had passed this law, the company could tell its employees: "Well, I have to live with this, I give it to you because the government is forcing me to do so." This is not how we shall create some sort of harmony between the unions and management.
I call on the good will of these owners to review entirely their philosophy concerning the attitude of unions. They must realize that, in 1974, unions are here to stay. They have a role to play and they do so. Of course as a politician, I have to face up to the consequences of this, the same as everyone else. What the unions are asking is not always convenient for us, but they have contributed greatly to social evolution in Canada. In their own way, through the mandates they have received, they have contributed to improve the situation of a great majority of the population.
If we can accept this, if we can stop looking for lawyers to study continuously the legal aspect of issues, the situation will improve. My colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out that whenever a lawyer is hired to look into a labour conflict issue, the problem remains unsolved for months. Mr. Speaker, the best example of this, I have witnessed in my constituency. The United Aircraft of Canada Limited hired the best lawyer, in other words the dirtiest they could find, to try to defend their cause. The workers have been on strike nine months and, according to the company, they will stay on strike for a long time. The company amuses itself by finding legal points to embarrass the union and not to solve the problem. The fact that they have 2,700 strikers on their hands, does not disturb them but let the strikers hire a good lawyer to represent them, that disturbs them. The

company keeps on doing research work and spends millions of dollars in fees to security agencies and all that kind of thing.
I might say in passing that I disapprove of that kind of employer that may be found in western Canada just as I do in my constituency. I believe it is immoral in 1974 not to be able to accept that a negotiating agent, duly commissioned by its members, duly accredited, be not held in respect. Those employers will never be respected by others.
Whenever employees are being prevented through their agent to accept negotiated settlements, it is bad. And it is still worse in this case because a conciliator makes recommendations, the union accepts them and the employer says that he does not accept them. Then the employers will come and say that unions contribute to the disruption of social order, Mr. Speaker. That is what they will say very soon. And it is the comment we often hear. If the employers really want to be held in respect by unions, they must also begin by showing respect for their employees and in order to do that, let them show respect to their negotiating agents.
Mr. Speaker, that is one of the best examples of employers who cannot adjust to the 1970's, who cannot adjust to social changes. That reminds me of a group of conservative men having a little business of their own, who want to preserve it and are anxious to keep their rights. They will have to learn that there are employees who allow them to make profits. If this is so I do not see why these employees should not benefit also.
Mr. Speaker, Dr. Perry's recommendations are minimum ones. In 1970 this was already being negotiated in Quebec. Now we have them in 1974.
I think it would be indecent to maintain here that we will contribute to inflation in Canada because we are giving a 15 per cent increase to some employees. There are bosses, Mr. Speaker, who will "screw" us for 60 per cent. And the bosses, the big consortiums, will "get" us even more by trying to "get" us with their income tax returns. You do not have to worry, that is where they make their money. And they are quite capable of doing this. After that, they tell us that because we are granting a 15 per cent raise we are contributing to inflation. They are really indecent.
We are quite lucky in Canada to have people who can respect the law and who are conscious of the fact that if they do not win there is a government who can support them. That is what is important.
I said before, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) really did good work in this case. I also said that I absolutely did not want government intervention between management and unions to become a normal procedure. I think that the Minister of Labour gave us an example of the patience one can have. All this started exactly on September 17, 1973 and we are now in October 1974. I think that the Minister of Labour has given both parties their chances and if management had really wanted to negotiate and accept Dr. Perry's recommendations we would not be in this position of being forced to vote a law to get respect for what is a vital minimum today.
Grain Handlers' Strike

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I would like first of all to compliment the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) for rising to make his maiden speech on such a contentious issue. I listened to him carefully. At the beginning of his speech he outlined the problem and said he regretted very much that parliament has to be the final negotiator in the conciliation and the bargaining process when the two parties were unable to reach agreement. I am sure all members of the House regret this also. But he failed to tell the House why the two parties have failed to reach an agreement in this particular dispute.
Normally when you have a labour dispute the two parties meet from time to time, and meaningful negotiations take place eventually when each party realizes that the other is seriously concerned. I have yet to hear why negotiations broke off, but I think the reason is obvious. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) has stayed out of this debate so far because his head is hanging low. He is the culprit. He is the person who deliberately intervened. As early as the first part of May he told the companies to settle for the Perry recommendation or the government would force it on them. It was at that point that meaningful negotiations ceased.
If I had been head of the labour union I would not have sat down to negotiate either. I would have known I had the government on my side and that, if I hung on long enough, the companies would be forced to accept what Perry recommended. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board erred in intervening as rapidly as he did.
I might accuse the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) of playing politics in trying to keep this sticky wicket away from the last election. He used section 81 of the Labour Act and said that there should be no walkout or strike for a period of two months after the election. That was within his power, and he had to do it because already the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board had destroyed any chance for meaningful negotiations.
Members of the Liberal Party can rise in this House and call the grain companies anything they like but they should recognize when the negotiations stopped; they stopped when the government intervened. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as I supposed he can do when he likes the minister who made the booboo, stepped in and supported the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. However, we have noticed a certain amount of demotion in the Liberal cabinet recently, and as suggested by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), there should be a few more.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) has done everything to destroy western Canada since he became a member of the cabinet. In the short time available this evening I want to point out that his actions during the time he has been a cabinet minister bear out his past actions. His first action was the well remembered LIFT program. Where did operation LIFT come from? It did not come from his brain; it is all outlined in the Canadian agricultural report submitted by the task force

on agriculture in 1969. It was dreamed up before he became minister.

speechtext:
The minister picked that idea out of that book and attempted to sell it to western Canada.
The minister can correct me if I am wrong. Wheat production fell by 150 million bushels in the following year. I may be out a little, Mr. Speaker, but the minister is indicating general approval of that figure. Any schoolboy can figure out how much wheat is worth today. Before August 1 at the elevator on delivery it was worth $3.50 a bushel. I hope the farmer gets $1.50 a bushel on final payment. A bushel should be worth $4 on a ball-park figure, so $600 million is what this minister has cost western farmers.
What did he do next? He brought in the grain stabilization bill. Parliament defeated that bill and saved western Canada millions of dollars. What was the next thing he did? He had a fire sale of barley across the world, selling at least 20 cents to 50 cents a bushel below the price he should have been getting. The minister nods his head in approval. He sold barley and failed to adjust the price of barley for a two month period.
The next thing he did was to devise a feed grains policy. The evidence is in the Canadian livestock report of 19721973. That policy cost the western feeder $50 per head for every animal he fed last winter. In an effort to bail out the western feeder this spring the government spent $3'/2 million per week subsidizing or supporting beef prices. One can figure that over 26 weeks that cost about $90 million.
Now let us look at the grain strike. The hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt asked the people in that constituency to vote for him. He is a minister in the cabinet, but I wonder if the people in Saskatoon-Humboldt realize that his position there has cost them millions and millions of dollars. I have already accounted for something like $700 million.
Let us look at April 10, 1974 and what Mr. Vogel, chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board, had to say about the rail strike. That strike was similar to what we had this summer. The minister failed to make his point in cabinet, and parliament should have acted long before he did. He failed to have any weight whatsoever in cabinet.
It is no wonder that many farm people believe the Wheat Board would fare better in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who has power in cabinet. The rail strike was brought before parliament, and what did it cost us? According to Mr. Vogel during the rail strike last year approximately 45,000 boxcars representing 95 million bushels were lost, and vessel demurrage charges cost producers of western Canada hundreds of thousands if not millions of dollars. This year he said, "No, we are not going to pay any demurrage charges; the government is not going to intervene there."

This holdout is because the companies could have settled it any time, at the government's price, acceptance of the Perry report recommendations. According to Mr. Vogel, in this particular strike demurrage charges alone will come to $18 million. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board suggests they will only be $10 million. I will make a little deal with him. Will the minister pick up everything over $10 million? If it is not going to be a cent over $10 million what has he got to lose? He does not call me on that one, and that is too bad.
We have gone down a whole list, Mr. Speaker-operation LIFT, grain stabilization, barley sales, a feed grains policy, and a railway strike which cost Canada millions of bushels of lost sales and millions of bushels of potential sales. Now we have the grain handlers' strike. It all began quite innocently, as do most wage negotiations. The companies and unions sparred a bit and felt one another out. The companies asked for a conciliator and the Minister of Labour appointed one. The conciliator did not bring in a final sealed document, but brought in a list of suggestions which might be used in reaching a settlement.
The government has blundered. The minister from Saskatoon-Humboldt has blundered. Recently we witnessed firings from the cabinet. I suggest that that minister should be demoted. He is too involved with questions of justice and abortions to have time for anything else.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
An hon. member says, "Wait until he deals with marijuana." Somebody also suggested that he may already be dealing with it. In any case, whom are we to believe. Some say that these workers will gain 61 per cent, but the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) says they will get only 15 per cent. Witnesses should come before the committee to clear up whether the increase is of the magnitude of 15 per cent, 41 per cent or 61 per cent. How is the COLA clause to be negotiated? We don't know, but we are asked to pass this bill on second reading tonight.
The Toronto Star of October 2 says that we have inflation by the bushel in Ottawa, that giving the Vancouver grain handlers 60 per cent over two years is inflationary.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his telegram to Mr. Runciman, President of United Grain Growers, said that the present settlement should not be considered as a precedent for wage settlements in other sectors of the economy, because the men in this dispute are trying to catch up with the longshoremen. Once they catch up, the longshoremen will go on strike to get ahead of the grain handlers.
The true test as to whether the companies have been the culprit in this matter is this: did they have difficulty in obtaining grain handlers? That will show whether they were stingy with regard to wages and working conditions. The answer is no. Grain handlers are available to any grain company operating on the west coast. So, Mr. Speaker, their pay has not been as bad as suggested by some speakers this afternoon.
Certainly the Prime Minister is wrong in suggesting this settlement will not set a precedent. It certainly will. The
October 7, 1974

government knows it will set a precedent. Grain inspectors at Vancouver who work for the same elevator companies the grain handlers work for, and who do much the same work as the grain handlers, will come out on strike next and demand a similar pay increase.
The government has offered them a niggardly 6 per cent. The Minister of Labour and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) know that 6 per cent more will not satisfy the grain inspectors. The Minister of Labour already knows, after the settlement affecting terminal workers at Thunder Bay and personnel working on ships in the St. Lawrence, that the 61 per cent figure has already become a guideline in Canadian wage settlements. He agreed to the settlement of those two disputes at 65 per cent and 69 per cent.
This evening we heard that the grain handlers will get only 15 per cent extra, not 65 per cent, as happened at the Lakehead. Of course the figure will vary, depending on whether it is applied to the top, bottom or middle of the wage scale. The grain companies have taken the average. Without doubt the reference of this matter to parliament has set a precedent for future parliaments. It is all very well to intervene and say there shall be no strike or walk out, but the point is this: meaningful negotiations cannot go on. There should be no intervention which prevents meaningful negotiation.
But the government intervened, and its intervention will cost the Canadian economy vast sums because the proposed settlement is inflationary. Further, this wage settlement will inspire similar wage settlements in future. They, too, will be inflationary. Frankly, I regret that parliament has been made the final arbitrator in this dispute. I think Dr. Perry should come before the committee and say how he interprets the COLA clause in the contract, or how he arrived at the COLA clause which will affect the grain handlers.
Years ago the grain handlers decided to do away with their own pension plan. They voluntarily did away with it in wage negotiations because the Canada Pension Plan had been introduced. Now they want their pension plan reinstated, with the companies to pay all the costs and the workers to pay none. Surely Dr. Perry could come before the committee so that it can determine how large is the increase that is being granted. Is the Toronto Star correct in alleging that in Ottawa there is inflation by the bushel, and that this is an increase of better than 60 per cent?
Like it or not, what the government does will set a precedent in wage settlements. It will affect inflationary pressures in this country. If the increase is to be only 15 per cent, it behooves members of the House to seek the proof of that; otherwise w.e shall merely be encouraging inflation. I shall be interested in hearing government supporters on this point. Are they prepared to have the matter clarified before the committee? We, as legislators, should know whether the increase is to be 61 per cent or 15 per cent. The matter should be cleared up. I hope this bill is sent to committee so that witnesses may be called to answer these questions fully.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Hamilton West told us how he had gone to Vancouver and Calgary and saw what was happening. I would have thought that on this occasion the hon. member and his party would have risen above partisanship and, on the floor of this House, sought a solution to the problem that now exists in Vancouver. However, I do not think members opposite are really interested in a solution.

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
I wish to quote from an article that appeared in the August 27 edition of the Vancouver Sun. British Columbia members of parliament were interviewed about whether parliament should be summoned to deal with this situation. I quote:
And Tory Ron Huntington-
He is the new Conservative member for Capilano.
-said Parliament should be called, but only to embarrass the Liberal government and not to resolve the grain strike situation-
"What's the point of having Parliament get involved now that the bargaining system has already been destroyed? But it would be tremendously embarrassing to the present government to have to call Parliament.
"On that basis, I would say, 'yes, call Parliament.' But I wouldn't want to see the government or the minister taking any discretionary action."
Asked if he was recommending that the government go to the effort of expense of calling the House in order to do nothing, Huntington said: "Yes, it would be very embarrassing to them. That's the only point of it all."
It is tragic that the hon. member for Hamilton West and his party should regard this situation not as one to seek a solution to a very serious work stoppage in Vancouver but to seek a partisan advantage. They seek to embarrass the government rather than to relieve the situation affecting the prairie wheat farmer and the Vancouver cargo handling facilities. I would have thought that in this new parliament we could have looked to Her Majesty's official opposition for a somewhat higher contribution to the debate and the resolution of these issues.
What the official spokesman of the Conservative party and the hon. member for Crowfoot have proposed today will not move one grain of wheat. It will not get one ship weighing anchor from English Bay. It is unfortunate that we have such a lack of leadership from the official opposition. This evening I appeal to them to forget that position, to be statesmanlike, to support this legislation, to get it to committee as quickly as possible, to get the work stoppage in the port of Vancouver over, and get the grain and ships moving again.
Here is a group that for a month has been saying "call parliament". They have been blaming the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for not calling parliament. We have now convened. We now have legislation. But they have adopted a policy which would make parliament impotent to deal with this particular situation. It is a truly deplorable situation and I hope the hon. member for Hamilton West will mend his ways during the course of the debate.
The bill before us is the usual type of bill for these unfortunate circumstances. My colleague explained it this afternoon. The bill contains five provisions, namely, that grain handling will be resumed, the collective agreement will be extended, the term of conciliation commissioner will be incorporated into the collective agreement, all strikes and walkouts are prohibited, and negotiations will resume on how the terms of the conciliation commissioner will be incorporated. Failing agreement on that, a referee will deal with the question. What the bill does can be examined in detail in committee, I hope tomorrow or the next day, when my colleague will appear before the committee.
One other point the hon. member for Hamilton West raised is that the bill did not set out that there would be
an industrial inquiry. He criticized the Minister of Labour for making that announcement today. The establishment of an industrial inquiry is set out in Sections 196 and 197 of the Canada Labour Code and need not be incorporated into this special legislation, Bill C-12. Therefore, in making his announcement this afternoon the Minister of Labour was acting in accordance with legislation already passed by parliament and which is already the law of the land. It was put forward by my colleague, the present Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey).
There is a need for this industrial inquiry into the whole history of labour management and grain handlers in Vancouver. The need is great. As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) said this afternoon, we do not want to come back next year, or the year after, and again have to pass legislation. As the minister said, we have seen a long and tedious history of labour management difficulties in the grain handler's situation at Vancouver.
We must seek a means of permanently establishing labour management stability in grain handling and cargo movement to and through the port of Vancouver. My colleague mentioned returning to the days of the dispute at the time of the St. Laurent government. For 21 years we have seen a history of mediators, conciliators, inquiry commissions of one sort or another, strikes, walkouts and labour management disturbances. In the interests of both parties and, more important, the interest of the national economy, the cause of the difficulty must be removed. We must resolve the underlying labour management difficulties.
It seems to me that an industrial inquiry as proposed by my colleague is a suitable instrument for initiating that kind of process. It would hear from all the parties concerned and, undoubtedly, it would take into account some of the constructive comments made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) this afternoon. It is essential that the underlying causes of unrest be removed.
The Port of Vancouver is the nation's busiest port. It is the second busiest in North America and the twelfth busiest in the world. Over the next five years we shall have to spend, depending upon what analysis one reads, anywhere between $500 million and $1 billion on upgrading marine facilities and access to the port. We cannot legitimately expect the public and the private sector to invest capital of this magnitude without taking steps to improve the labour-management climate in the port. It seems to me this is the whole purpose of the two-pronged approach proposed by the government through the Minister of Labour.
First, the bill before us ought to be passed as quickly as possible so that operations in the port can be resumed. Secondly, from a longer term point of view, there should be an inquiry into the whole history of labour-management in the hope of producing permanent solutions and creating healthy industrial relations. I hope the commissioner will be imaginative in the way he looks at his terms of reference, and that he will suggest to all the parties involved long term solutions to the problems which have

October 7, 1974

vexed wheat shippers and all others engaged in port operations. I hope the official opposition and its spokesmen will recognize that it is essential to pass this legislation quickly and that they will forego what is an obvious delight to them, that is, an attempt to derive some partisan advantage at the expense of the Minister of Labour, or of the Wheat Board, or of the government.
