speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Listening to the unctuous tones of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) I looked across the aisle expecting to see a halo above his shiny visage. I heard him attack Her Majesty's loyal opposition for showing partisanship, and call upon us for statesmanship, in fact demand from us all the things which he and his colleagues have failed to produce. It seems to me he wants us to endorse the clumsy solution which is being foisted upon the country by the government and, in the process, somehow, to accept responsibility for it. I say to the minister: This is your baby; don't expect us to look after it.
As one of the members chosen to go to the beautiful city of Vancouver to look into the background of the situation, I did so with a certain advantage. Like the government, I did not know very much about the subject. And as I looked into the various ramifications of the matter, and spoke to the parties involved, I quickly learned that this was an extremely complex human issue. We were able to speak with union members and their negotiating team led by Mr. Henry Kanes who, I may say, personally impressed me a great deal.
We found that, unlike some other less progressive unions, this one was anxious to come to grips with the challenge of moving grain more quickly through the Port of Vancouver. We found that the union was interested in discussing working conditions, new methods of processing grain and cleaning it on the prairies, and the introduction of equipment which will speed the unloading of cars at the terminals. In other words, there was a great willingness to participate in a team approach, using what one could call, I suppose, an approach by way of industrial democracy, leading to all kinds of long term solutions, adopted in a constructive way in co-ordination with the management of the companies and prairie agricultural interests.
Also, we found that management were most concerned about certain questions which were fundamental in their eyes, which meant they had to take account of past history, and of what had happened to the farmers on the prairies in the bad years when some of those who grew the grain received less by way of remuneration than those who handled it at the elevators and expedited its passage to world markets.
It is said there is nothing altogether new and that if one examines the background of any situation one will find in the past a parallel to what is occurring in the present. So I
Grain Handlers' Strike
took the opportunity to do some research. I go back to the Liberal administration led by Alexander Mackenzie in 1877. The Governor-General, Lord Dufferin, said at that time in a speech at the City Hall in Winnipeg, on September 29:
You have been blessed with an abundant harvest, and soon I trust will a railway come to carry to those who need it the surplus of your produce, now-as my own eyes have witnesses-imprisoned in your storehouses for want of the means of transport.
Well, today we find that a vast amount of Canada's grain reserves are still imprisoned in a storehouse, or, more precisely, in the great grain terminals on the west coast and there is no way because of a strike or lock-out, in which we can transport them to our customers and to the hungry people of the world. This is a deplorable situation and it seems to me that implicit in this situation is the government's failure to demonstrate any degree of statesmanship. For if statesmanship had been shown, the present situation would never have developed.
I suggest there is a natural alliance between the prairie farmers, who do such a fine job of growing our wheat, and the people on the west coast, who do such a fine job handling it, and that there is a great deal of room for the benefits of productivity to be brought into effect as was stated by my hon. friend, the Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), the minister of agriculture in the regime of my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in his excellent speech this afternoon. It is unfortunate that in recent years no one on the government side has made any attempt to bring these two groups of people together for the benefit of themselves and of the nation.
The transportation system necessary to the movement of these vast quantities of wheat has become obsolescent; the collection system on the prairies has become obsolescent. Now we see that labour-management relations between the two groups have also become absolescent. It is clear that in this country, one of the greatest wheat and grain producers in the world, we can no longer deliver our harvest to customers abroad because the government cannot give leadership or devise a formula for setting up a proper climate for industrial relations.
That sincere people like the grain handlers in Vancouver, management and the owners-presidents, if you will-of the terminals, who reside on the prairies, cannot come together for the common good of all is one of the biggest tragedies of the whole affair, at least to me as a member who has not been too close to the situation but who has the benefit of looking at the situation without any preconceived ideas.
I should like to say something about the transportation aspects of the matter. Only a few months ago eastern Canadian agriculture was jeopardized by the lack of transportation facilities to move feed grains to this particular part of the country. The mismanagement of the transportation system of the country has had the end result of placing an increased burden on consumers in the form of higher prices. For example, let me look at the feed grain supplies in eastern Canada.
190

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
We forget, perhaps within the confines of this debate, that there was an equally serious labour dispute involving the Great Lakes terminals, which in turn had a direct effect not only in that particular region of the country but in the extreme eastern region of Canada as well. Roger Perrault, chairman of the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, expects difficulties. This is what he said in a recent news release:
The system will have to operate smoothly from now to the end of the Great Lakes navigation season to get enough domestic feed grain into position for normal movement during the winter months. Otherwise, eastern Canadian farmers may have to pay the extra cost for moving more grain than usual by rail and there could be shortages of some grains in certain areas if there are further delays and interruptions in the movement... Since feed grains are a major component in the production of milk, poultry, eggs and meat, consumers should not expect lower price tags on these food items in the year ahead.
Difficulties in labour-management relations not only had serious repercussions on our international sales-and these difficulties were very adequately dealt with by the members who have spoken here today. Our country not only lost credibility as a reputable supplier of this vitally needed commodity, grain; our internal economy has also been seriously affected. This makes it all the more important that something be done by the government along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, and hinted at by the Minister of National Revenue. What we need is something constructive, statesmanlike if you will, that finally will allow labour and management to participate jointly in finding what I refer to as some sort of industrial democratic solution.
It is obvious that not all industries offer the same opportunities for productivity that will lower the cost of settlements relative to inflation, as is the case with the present grain handlers' strike. Some industries have a greater labour content and are more marginal. But surely here in grain handling there is the type of situation where there is a real and obvious gain to be made by invoking productivity, perhaps marrying to some extent COLA and productivity, in an attempt to come to some sort of innovative solution. Surely there must be some greater initiative to be shown than is shown by this bill we are discussing tonight.
This bill, while necessary in the present context to break the logjam, or perhaps I should say the wheat jam, and get this commodity flowing again, does nothing else. It illustrates by its content that there is nothing, shall I say, contemplated of an imaginative nature to settle any future difficulties. The provision in clause 7 for appointing a referee is, as far as I am concerned, a sort of built-in admission of the fact that there will undoubtedly be difficulties in interpreting this clause, which as I recall embodies the fringe benefits that are set out in the Perry report, a report that was treated, or mistreated as if he were cast as an arbitrator.
If this bill offered any sort of innovative approach or promised some particular solution to this unfortunate situation, then I would have no trouble supporting it. But all it is in fact is some sort of self-destruct mechanism. What is going to happen is that these kinds of large settlements will inevitably be reflected in the economy.
The Canadian Manufacturers Association, for example, are this evening registering great concern about what is

going to happen to negotiations in the private sector as a result of this legislation. The very magnitude of some of these settlements that parties are driven to, because of the government's failure to bring forward some sort of general inflation policy, will only help increase the inflationary spiral and thus erode the very gains workers have achieved, leaving everyone worse off, particularly those who are not unionized and who have not been able to protect themselves by getting similar types of large settlements. So what we have is nothing more nor less than a vicious circle, and the situation is exacerbated by the difficulties that a country our size is having with its transportation system.
Pretty soon, both on the Great Lakes and on the west coast, longshoremen will be out on strike unless there is some greater ingenuity shown than has been shown in the dealings with the grain handlers. Then it will be the turn of the railway workers. Although I sincerly hope this will not be the case, there could be difficulties with the postal workers. Indeed, there could be difficulties with the whole broad spectrum of the Canadian work force. Yet all we can do tonight in parliament is to bring in a bill which to a certain extent is dictatorial and coercive. It does not even have the virtue of giving the parties at least something of what they wanted leaving the rest to be decided by continuing negotiations.
It has been suggested that if the wage demands were split, and the union given $1.30 or $1.40 increase, which is something in the vicinity of what its members were asking originally, and another arbitrator were appointed to negotiate some of the fringe benefits, then we as parliamentarians at least would not be acting dictatorially and telling these people what is fair. Certainly I do not know what is fair, and I suggest that many of my colleagues in this House do not know what is fair either.
We are sitting here as the highest court in the land purporting to deal with something that is vital to the lives and livelihoods of workers, something that is going to affect the industrial management-labour complex of this country. Yet we do not have the necessary expertise collectively to make this judgment. This is a task for people with greater background experience than many of us in this House have, though perhaps there are some who do have this experience. That is why I object to this particular procedure used by the government, and why I cannot support this particular bill.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second time during my short experience in this House that parliament has been called upon to legislate men back to work. I find that a disagreeable duty, as do my colleagues in this House. It is also disagreeable to see the kind of political manoeuvring that is taking place here in order to gain points, to gain advantage over the plight of the working people of this country.
When this House legislated workers in our railway system back to work the members of the Conservative party were quite eager, as were the members of the Liberal party, to offer a wage settlement that was far below what a conciliation officer recommended. Today we find a variation on that theme. Today we find a conciliator who has recommended a wage settlement still below what the
October 7, 1974

workers wanted, but to which the companies have violently objected.
We heard the Conservative member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), and others, come out very strongly on the side of the companies, using the argument that the whole system is inflationary and that the workers were not bargaining in good faith. It is very disturbing to me to see that kind of politicking going on rather than an examination of the issue on its merits.
Let me review for the consideration of this House why we find ourselves in this situation today. This cannot be expressed better than it was by Mr. Perry in his letter to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) on April 22, 1974 as follows:
As it has now become clear to me that the differences in expectations between the contracting parties-arising from a series of accumulated past issues as well as the special, inflationary circumstances of 1974- remain too wide to be resolved through further conciliatory efforts, I am, therefore, submitting for your consideration some suggestions which, hopefully, might form a basis upon which the two parties could, ultimately, enter into a two-year agreement.
If we stop playing political games and are honest with ourselves in wanting to get the wheat moving again, and to do something just for the workers in the elevators in Vancouver, we should start by asking ourselves why these negotiations broke down. I submit that the blame for the breakdown in these negotiations lies primarily with the companies, and I should like to outline why I say that.
For collective bargaining to work there must be an understanding and a willingness on both sides that there be a settlement at some point in time. Each side is going to argue very vigorously for its cause, but there has to be that fundamental willingness to settle. I do not see that willingness when I look at the history of these negotiations. What I see is the grain handlers' union being frustrated, not only by the circumstances under which the men work but by the attitude of the companies, to the point that they have been forced finally to take strike action.
First of all, what are the components of this frustration? If we examine the working conditions in those elevators in Vancouver we discover low morale among the working men. There is a problem with excessive dust. The companies have installed machinery to extract the dust, but it is not working properly. Much of the dust remains in the elevators, with the result that the men work under very unhealthy conditions.
We also find a shortage of the facilities one would take for granted in any enlightened area of employment, such as a shortage of showers, toilets and lunchroom facilities. The companies are using damping chemicals which have proven to be a hazard to health because of their nature and the lack of exhaust venting facilities. We also find many documented examples of unsafe working conditions in these elevators. In addition, there is evidence of inefficient management and inefficient operation in the companies' attempt to automate the elevators.
We have here a group of workers who are cognizant of the responsibility to move grain, working under condi-
Grain Handlers' Strike
tions which have continuously deteriorated, but which they have brought to the attention of management. They have seen their suggested improvements continuously rejected. When we consider the companies' attitude toward working conditions we see a lack of care and understanding. More important, when we look at the attitude of the companies toward negotiations it becomes evident that they have been using obstructionist tactics.
There have been four occasions during the last 14 years when negotiations between the elevator workers and the companies have gone the route of conciliation. On four occasions the conciliation reports have been accepted by the union but rejected by the companies. This must be borne in mind before we place the blame on one side or the other too quickly.
Let us look at the history of negotiation and decide who have been the obstructionists. I maintain it has been the companies. During the present dispute the companies terminated welfare and other benefits which had already been established and included in past contracts. Obviously there is not just a dispute in respect of wages, because the welfare and fringe benefits that had been established under previous contracts were suspended. That can only be interpreted by the working person to be harassment and obstruction.
There have been constructive attempts by the negotiators for the unions to put their position to the ultimate owners of the co-operatives, namely, the farmers. This includes the suggestion to management that there should be a farmer representative, as an observer only, at the negotiating table. These suggestions have been rejected out of hand by the companies.
The employers on this occasion asked for conciliation when the report was brought in. Once again the companies rejected this. The companies have refused to accept Mr. Perry's report even though they knew full well, as a result of statements by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), that parliament would eventually legislate the report into law. What kind of an attitude is that? I suggest it is an attitude of obstruction and nothing else.
I wonder whether the companies would have been so willing to continue this delay by not accepting the conciliation report if they had been shipping flax and rape-seed through these elevators rather than wheat, particularly in view of the fact that the companies have to pay demurrage charges in respect of flax and rapeseed whereas the Canadian Wheat Board has to pay the demurrage charge on wheat?
When one looks at the attitude of these grain companies it becomes very evident who is responsible for the breakdown in the collective bargaining in this situation. I have on my desk some very glossy publications by the grain companies regarding the cost of this wage settlement. I might say that there has been a great campaign carried on in the newspapers, as well as on television and radio. Let us examine the situation to see whether the cost of this settlement is as inflationary as the companies maintain.
First of all, the companies have claimed that the cost will be $3.03 an hour above the present base rate of $4.96 an hour, inclusive of pensions, cost of living and wage benefits. They have claimed that the increase would be 61
28305-13?!

October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
per cent. That was their original claim, and this resulted in headlines to the effect that the settlement would be extraordinarily inflationary. We now know that the same companies, having done some further calculations suggested to them by their officials, have revised this increase from 61 per cent to 48 per cent. The unions have also bandied some figures around. They claimed that the total cost would be $2.20 an hour, or an increase of 44 per cent.
Even if you take the company figure, or the union figure, and work out the actual cost of this wage settlement per bushel of wheat, the range is somewhere between three quarters of one cent and one cent per bushel. Is that supposed to be inflationary?
If we look at the Perry report and the whole problem that was exposed in it of the inefficiency of handling grain in those elevators, it would seem to me that that one cent per bushel could easily be made up by the union and management sitting down together and working out a more efficient way of handling the grain. They have tried some automation but it has worked very badly because of poor installation and management. If the two sides, in the interests of the Canadian public, got together and worked out a more efficient handling of that grain, this increase could be absorbed in increased sales and exports; it would not be inflationary.
If we consider the Perry report, the wage factor alone amounts to a 15 per cent increase a year. What do you expect the working man in Canada in whatever area or whatever union to settle for when the cost of living alone in this past year has risen by 11 per cent? Is a 15 per cent wage increase in those circumstances inflationary? He is running just to stand still.
What is so galling to these men working in the elevators and on the docks is the fact that they are working side by side with longshoremen who, in many cases, are doing similar work and being paid more. If that is not a frustrating experience, I do not know what is. How many of us here in this House would be willing to accept a differential in pay because of our kind of job or the number of hours we are working? It should be similar pay for similar work.
Let us look at the difference between the longshoremen and the grainhandlers. The basic wage rate for the grain workers is now $4.96 an hour. Under the Perry report, in the first year that would rise to $5.83 an hour. What are the longshoremen getting who are working beside these grain handlers? They are getting $6.08 an hour. May I remind this House that at the end of November the longshoremen's contract comes up for renegotiation, and again they will be seeking a higher settlement. So here you have grain workers today getting paid $4.96 an hour while longshoremen working beside them receive $6.08 an hour. That is obviously unjust and discriminatory.
The pension plan is also, for those who care to look at it, very different between the two groups. The recommendation in the Perry report is that the employer contribute 25 cents an hour for the pension of the grain handler. Already the longshoremen receive a contribution from their employer of 53 cents an hour. If you look at the overtime rate between the two groups, again you see vast discrimi-

nation and vast differences between double time and time and a half.
What these men are asking seems to me very fair- comparable pay for comparable work. It seems to me then that these men have a just case. Their arguments make sense and it is the duty of the House to pass this legislation quickly, not only so that they can at least get a just settlement but so that the grain can begin to move in this country and the economy get back on the right track. I cannot for the life of me understand the attitude of my colleagues in the Conservative party who will vote against the bill and at the same time want a prolonged debate all night on it. They want the standing committee to call various witnesses before it to prolong the situation, the settlement of which they demanded all summer.
These men are playing politics, and the government is playing politics in delaying the settlement of this issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of regret that I rise to speak in this debate. I think that most members of the House were hoping that the whole situation would have been solved some time ago. Then it was indicated this afternoon, and also this evening, that if it had not been for the government, mainly the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) but also the minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang), we would have had a settlement by now and we would not have to spend time dealing with this matter in the House.
We have spoken much this afternoon and this evening about the various aspects of the strike, but as yet we have not really referred to the cost of that strike to the people whom it will affect. The first ones whom it will affect are the western Canadian farmers, although it goes without saying that this strike will have repercussions right across our whole economy.
Mention has been made about the kind of demurrage charge that the Wheat Board will have to pay. Ultimately, if the Canadian Wheat Board has to pay, it comes out of the final payment alloted to farmers. Let me quote from an editorial in the Vancouver Sun of August 19 in which it is stated that, according to reliable reports from the Canadian Wheat Board, the cost could range anywhere from $10 million to $15 million, a record demurrage charge this year.
It goes on to say:
The largest demurrage in the past amounted to $2.4 million for the crop year 1972-73.
The article goes on to say that we have agents for various boat companies that were chartered to haul Canadian grain. One ship is called Aquafaith. The article says:
Agents for the Aquafaith, which arrived in port on July 5-and was on demurrage for 36 days before she was fully loaded for China, say
October 7, 1974

demurrage will come to $240,000. Demurrage on the Aquaglory, which arrived July 9, amounts to $200,000, they say.
The Kinko Manx waited 24 days and cost the Wheat Board $144,000 before she finally departed on Friday.
This money will come directly out of the farmers' pockets in the end, and anybody who says that this strike will not be costly first and foremost to the Canadian farmers is not telling the whole truth.
A second important consideration is the loss of world reputation which Canada will suffer. This has certainly been noted before by various people. I think there is no doubt that we are talking of a situation in which, at present, there are four countries out of 151 that export grain to the rest of the world. Canada is one of those four countries, the others being Argentina, Australia and the United States. Along with the loss in world reputation we have a moral obligation to move grain to feed the world at a time in which famine and starvation are becoming widespread.
The previous speaker alluded to the fact that the only crop that was moved out of Vancouver on which we certainly lost was wheat. That is not true. We have loss of other sales-not necessarily deferred sales, but actual loss of sales.
I have before me a copy of the "Rapeseed Digest" dated October, 1974 which is published by the Rapeseed Association of Canada every month. In it appears the statement:
Canada's new parliament met on September 30, but even if the labour problems are given a high priority on the calendar of the House of Commons, it appears doubtful that work will be resumed before mid-October. In the meantime, European suppliers of rapeseed have cut deeply into the market in Japan, with sales reported to total 175,000 metric tons, the equivalent of 7.7 million bushels, all for shipment before the end of 1974.
This loss of market will not be recovered by Canada in the 1974-75 crop year.
These are just some of the ramifications of the situation, in addition to what has been said earlier this evening, Mr. Speaker.
Personally I feel that the interference of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) in this situation is unforgiveable. When we were in Vancouver we were told that if the government had not stepped in there might have been a chance to settle the strike if the two parties could have got down to meaningful bargaining.
The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) also has to bear some of the blame. On the one hand he is acting in the interests of the farmers, although on this particular issue I think he sold western Canadian farmers down the drain by condoning what was done by the Minister of Labour. It seems apparent he only works for the farmers when it is politically advantageous to do so. That situation cannot continue, Mr. Speaker.
This strike is unique in that it raises the question of parity with longshoremen. I have here a copy of a telegram sent by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the President of the United Grain Growers on August 14. The telegram says in part:
Without accepting your figures, we would agree that the settlement is costly. However, your representations and those made previously on
Grain Handlers' Strike
your behalf by your senior management, fail to take into account the unique aspects of this situation. You must have been informed by your labour relations advisers of the issue of parity with longshoremen performing similar tasks to members of local 333 on the same waterfront. This factor must have been one which influenced the content of the conciliation commissioner's report. Moreover, this factor, which is unique to this particular dispute, means that the settlement proposed by Dr. Perry should not set a precedent for other wage settlements in other sectors of the economy.
In the area of parity a valid question would be why the companies should be forced, by a report which was admitted to be inconclusive, to accept parity for two such separate groups as grain handlers and longshoremen? It is commonly accepted all over the world that they do different work and have different working conditions. Longshoremen really do not have an assurance of steady employment.
It is remarkable that the government only saw fit to offer the Vancouver grain inspectors of the Canadian Grain Commission, who work side by side with grain handlers, a 6 per cent wage increase over 18 months and a 5.5 per cent increase over the following 12 months. No wonder Mr. C. W. Lewis, chairman of the bargaining committee of Local 60, asked Mr. Trudeau on August 22 that the basic wage of grain inspectors be "at least parity with all Vancouver grain workers". This justifies the stand that the Perry report is just a springboard for increased inflation across the country. It certainly shoots down the argument that this is a unique and special kind of settlement. I believe the Minister of Labour has said that publicly before.
The Perry report is being resisted for one real reason. As I understand it, the companies wanted to have the Perry report discussed in parliament because they wanted the government to put its money where its mouth is.
The government admits that inflation is the number one problem, and approves of a settlement which will award an additional $3.03 an hour to 550 grain handlers. You can call it a 61 per cent increase over two years if you are comparing it with the basic wage of $4.96, or you can call it a 52 per cent increase if you are comparing the $3.03 increase in wages, cost of living, pensions and fringe benefits, with the former package.
Regardless of the percentages, a 50 per cent increase, with no increase in productivity in terms of goods and services, if applied to everyone in this country, simply drops our dollar value by one third in two years. I believe this settlement will be an inflationary signal to all labour, organized and unorganized-every one. Any time you discuss an inflationary settlement in a fishbowl as this one has certainly been, it becomes a very real target to everyone else. It is not surprising in view of the publicity that has been given to the settlement because of the intervention by the government, that an emotional impact is felt all across the country when discussing the Perry report and its ramifications. In the long run this may have great impetus and fuel the fires of inflation in the next year, or year and a half.
We have a precedent that has been cited already. Only eight years ago Prime Minister Pearson sanctioned that famous 30 per cent seaway employees' award. At that time it was not considered inflationary but it did serve as a goal for everyone else, and inflation took off.



October 7, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
We have talked a lot tonight about the effects on different people in this country. I think first and foremost it is the farmers who feel the effects. It would be interesting to hear what three or four of them have said about the strike, the grain companies' demands and the government's response to holding the line in the strike. I have a letter here from a farmer in Fincastle, Alberta who says:
We are inflating our money so rapidly that it is threatening the stability of our money. If we have any part to play in setting a base of inflation of 61 per cent over two years, it will mean we helped to destroy all confidence in our money and we all know what that means to all of our society.
I received other letters over the past few weeks. A farmer from Kelvington-Nut Mountain, Saskatchewan writes:
If the grain handlers get this increase the farmers will be paying it in the final end. Along with all other labour forces increases. Is Mr. Trudeau then going to give us a 61 per cent subsidy on grain? It is high time that the government faced this inflation issue and did something constructive about it, instead of by fuelling it.
There are many more letters to the same effect and I suppose all members of the House are getting them. These farmers are very very concerned, as are all segments of society, over what is happening to the economy and the way inflation is going.
It may well be asked why grain farmers feel this way when they are earning the highest income in their history. Without being disrespectful to those in other occupations, I think farmers are probably more sensitive than others to inflation, because they have tightened their belts many times during the past 25 or 30 years. Grain farmers are sensitive to the costs of those items they must buy in order to grow a bushel of grain. Land is less of a factor in costs today.
Did you ever think how the farmer is hit by inflation? He has to buy his fertilizer, other chemicals and machinery. When the prices of those go up, his grain becomes more expensive to grow; yet grain prices do not necessarily go up by an amount equal to his increased cost, because he is competing on the world market. Actually there is some indication that grain prices will come down in the next year or 18 months. Costs of production are a most important factor for farmers today, because they face what may be the severest cost-price squeeze in history.
What will happen after the strike is settled at Vancouver? I hope it is settled as quickly as possible. We want to see grain moving from the port again. As I say, what will happen after the strike is settled?

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: That shouldn't be too hard to figure out. Look into your crystal ball.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
My crystal ball tells me that productivity in the port of Vancouver will be low. I say that because labour-management relations, poor as they were previously, had degenerated even more this past summer.
When the Conservative caucus committee went to Vancouver it was impressed with the attitude of the union which talked of modernizing rail traffic to the port and of modernizing port operations. The union wanted to be involved in the work being done. Unless the two sides can

come together after the strike is settled and improve relationships, the future looks bleak. If the two sides do not come together, if labour-management strife in Vancouver continues, our exports of wheat which have been steadily dropping during the past few years will decline even more. Our percentage of sales on the world market will be even smaller that it is now. For the good of the entire economy, productivity at Vancouver must be raised. This is a must.
We must also encourage the heads of the grain companies and of the unions to get together and find meaningful ground for discussion of common problems, because there are common problems. Unless we do that, the future looks bleak. If we do that then there will be a future for the continuing movement of grain through the port of Vancouver.

speechtext:
Hon. members have talked about the problem we faced in this country as we watched the process of labour negotiations come down to the wire, so to speak. We took note of the final phases of negotiation and of the conciliation report.
October 7, 1974

That report was made after the parties had failed to reach agreement. It was issued in a case in which, as even the most unbiased observer would agree, there had been a bad history of labour-management relations. If I may say so, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) was too diplomatic to say himself, the history of bad labour-management relations has arisen largely because of the way in which the companies had negotiated over many years in the past.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) said that when he was in Vancouver somebody told him if we had stayed away from the matter a little longer it would soon have been settled. I ask, who told him that? No doubt a representative of a company told him. In view of the bad history of labour-management relations, we saw the possibility of a strike. Of course, the conciliation report, drawn up in those circumstances, is bound to be an important factor in any future settlement.
We took action under the Canada Labour Code, action which was provided for only three or four years ago. This allowed us, because we were in the middle of an election campaign and therefore in no position to deal with the strike, to postpone the period in which a strike or walk out might occur legally until one month after the writs for return were in.
The interesting thing to note is this: although one can go through the process of postponing the legal time in which a walk out or strike can occur, one cannot with that process make workmen work, or make employers maintain them on the job. Even when there was no talk of a walk out or strike, the port of Vancouver, in May, and for three or four months previously, had been working at about half speed. While some may blame the present situation on the dissatisfaction of the men because of their relationship with the companies, or on the attitude of the companies, the fact is that unless you maintain an atmosphere of goodwill you will not keep a business working. You will not keep it going simply by declaring that something is illegal and not to be done.
It is the goodwill of the situation that is important. We saw this situation and we saw that the port would likely be closed even if we had, as we did, exercised the power under the Canada Labour Code to postpone the date for a legal strike or shutdown. We thought it was important to indicate to the men and the companies, whom we believed would be interested in maintaining the port open, that if in the end they did not reach a settlement, which we hoped they would continue to reach for, we saw the inevitability of what Dr. Perry had recommended in his report as the basis for final settlement.
That led us to think we should have the port working all out full time. As the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) stated, we regret that that did not happen. Even in the period before August 23 the port was partly idle and demurrage charges totalling $3 million piled up during that time.
What amazed me is that in these circumstances the companies refused to sit down and negotiate with the Perry report as the basis. They chose to go about the country, at least the farming community, taking from the
Grain Handlers' Strike
Perry report every possible ambiguity, or even less than ambiguity, and twisting it to the extreme possible against their interest in order to come up with this figure of 61 per cent. I repeat they had to twist it against their interest.
I said earlier they seemed to be trying in that way to coast in on some of the talk about inflation that was going on in the country at that time. Everyone recognizes now that that figure is ridiculous in relation to the Perry report. The figure is in fact significantly below that.
We talk about percentages. We, especially those in this place, should appreciate that without examining the base and the circumstances, as Dr. Perry has done, percentages are meaningless. If the farmers have had a rapid increase in percentage terms in the amount they get for wheat or barley, until they get to the point where they are finally getting what they deserve, is there any point in talking about a 100 per cent increase from $1.70 to $3.40? Of course not. You have to look at the realistic situation around you in order to judge. That is where we stand today. We stand here with a good deal of talk about the losses that have been suffered in this strike.
There have been significant losses to the farmer. We have said this from the beginning. I mentioned the $3 million in demurrage charges. This is probably related to the months of slowdown. Let me say at once that relating demurrage to a specific cost is very complicated. Therefore, it will never be satisfactorily or finally settled.
I am simply relying on the best estimates the wheat board can give me. It still concludes today that another $7 million, in addition to that $3 million, may be associated with the actual close-down of the port. That means a total loss to the farmers, mainly through the Canadian Wheat Board but also in connection with the other grains, of $10 million.
There have been some rather broad and sweeping statements about the losses. There have been statements about losses of goodwill. I regret the difficulty we cause our good customers by not being able to deliver when they expect grain from us. However, let me say that this year we happen to be extremely fortunate in that we have such a sellers' market. We may have time to build the goodwill. It may be very difficult to put a specific figure on losses.
We are also told about lost sales. As we sit here at this point in time, I think that can be discounted. We have seen the example of the demand, unfulfilled, from the Soviet Union. We can see the kind of demand there is throughout the world. It will allow us to move as great an amount of grain as we can, notwithstanding the close-down. That was not necessarily foreseen. No one could have predicted that in April or May. However, we can now say that that is how it will be.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) put another figure down for this lost sale, although it seems to be for the same grain we did not sell when we had the railway strike, or when we had the snow and ice a few years previously. He keeps managing to recycle that unsold grain. I intend to put a little pile in front of him some day and say, "There is the grain you talk about that we did not sell all this time." It is our good fortune that that is probably not a real cost. But we are left with the

October 7, 1974
Adjournment Debate
$10 million, still a significant figure any way you look at it.
Once the government had taken the position it did, why did the companies allow this strike to happen? I can understand them waiting before July 8 because they may have hoped something different would happen and they would be faced with a new ballgame. However, in the month following that, they really had no reason at all.
I would like to observe that among the losers in this strike are the men who have lost their time and wages, and the farmers who have lost through the significant demurrage charges. However, the losers do not necessarily include the grain companies. This year they will likely move every bushel they would have moved in terms of throughput with or without this strike. They will likely store more grain because it will be there a little longer than it would have been without the strike. They will not be the losers.
My hope in urging them to settle was based on the fact that the most significant among them are in fact farmer-owned. I thought they should have been sujected to the fact that the losses to the farmers would be significant and should be counted in their calculations. That was not to be. Therefore, we are here this evening with this legislation, legislation in practical terms, inevitable in its terms once the independent conciliator had brought down his report. I therefore say to hon. members at this late hour, one minute before 10 o'clock, let this bill have second reading now, go to committee, and let's get on with the work without further partisanship.

HOUSING-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES TO EXPAND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to bring the Minister of State for

Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) back into the House at this late hour.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES TO EXPAND PROGRAMS
speechtext: I haven't left yet.

subtopic: HOUSING-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES TO EXPAND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I especially regret it because I know how hard he is working to bring more housing to Newfoundland. On October 1 I asked the minister about the progress being made to implement various programs under the National Housing Act, particularly insofar as they refer to the Neighbourhood Improvement Program, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and the rural and native housing program. While I appreciate the reply he gave, the urgency of the situation dictates further clarification.
The situation is not only urgent, it is desperate. I requested an adjournment debate, Mr. Speaker, because it is impossible to elaborate on a question in the House in the time allotted to us. Incidentally this should be the subject of consideration when we are talking about reforms in the House of Commons, to which reference was made in the Speech from the Throne.
Since the announcement of the aforementioned programs I have been a strong advocate of them but was naive enough to think they would come into effect within a reasonable period of time. However, all I have experienced is frustration in dealing with the various elements which fall within the minister's responsibility, and I continue to receive answers which do nothing more than emphasize the need for rethinking our priorities.
The RRAP program, for example, provides loans for citizens in the low income brackets. Those whose income is $6,000 or below can qualify for a loan of up to $5,000 with 50 per cent being forgiven. This is fine. It is exemplary, it is wonderful, and I give the government full marks for its introduction. But after 15 months virtually nothing has been produced.
I am sure the minister will tell us once again that the consultative process is going on to speed up its implementation. Nevertheless, here we are, some 15 months after the amendments to the National Housing Act were introduced, and little or nothing has been accomplished. A member who troubles to make inquiries receives only the usual excuses in letters such as the following which I received from the President of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In a letter dated September 17, 1974, Mr. William Teron stated:
Thank you for your letter of August 23 concerning Neighbourhood Improvement and Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Programs.
As you are no doubt aware, RRAP is to be delivered in two separate approaches; one in the urban context linked with NIP and the other as an element of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's Rural and Native Housing Program. Under the 1974 NIP agreement between the federal government and the Province of Newfoundland, $1.34 million is provided for activity under this program. Of this total, $639,000 was approved last June for Corner Brook and we anticipate the remainder will be allocated very shortly for St. John's. In both instances, the funds will be used to complete projects financed under the old urban renewal provisions of the National Housing Act. In all likelihood, the delays to which you referred were engendered by the necessity of identifying and recasting older proposals so that they could meet NIP and RRAP objectives.
October 7, 1974

He went on to say that he shared my concern. That is what we hear all the time. They share your concern, but nothing happens. I shall not go into details of further complaints. All I wish to do is help the minister by placing before him a number of suggestions.
Since we are in a period of oil crisis I maintain that a great contribution could be directed toward helping those living on low and fixed incomes in many thousands of homes across Canada by immediately implementing standards across Canada to include, as a priority, the immediate insulation of homes which are substandard in quality, thereby reducing the wastage of home heating fuels.
Similarly, in the Province of Newfoundland it is necessary that the province increase the fuel allowance during the colder months of the year due to the fact that it is impossible for those receiving social assistance to cope with fuel costs. The federal government has to pay 50 per cent of this cost.
Home-owners living on welfare cannot possibly maintain their homes properly at a time when the cost of building materials is so high. I can only say that not only would both levels of government save millions of dollars in housing repairs; they would also save millions of gallons of heating fuel now being wasted.
The answer is not only to treat this RRAP program on a priority basis but to direct meaningful action, initiated by the minister, and demand that the $10 million now allocated be increased to a realistic figure. In addition, the necessary steps must be taken to expand this very worthwhile program as an emergency measure and thereby contribute toward relieving a critical area of shortage in Canada. Lastly, we should specifically provide a stop gap to the need for new housing, a need that is difficult to cope with under present circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barnett J. Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES TO EXPAND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the interesting suggestions put forward by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). He suggested there have been undue delays in implementing both NIP and RRAP. We have made tremendous headway in bringing these new programs into operation. First of all, in the case of NIP, the neighbourhood improvement program, we have signed the necessary agreements with nine of the ten provinces so far and expect to sign the tenth agreement very soon. Under these agreements we are allocating more than $40 million to the provinces for this program.
The provinces have since selected the municipalities, and a total of 64 municipalities are proceeding with neighbourhood improvement programs. Altogether these municipalities have now selected 33 neighbourhoods, and the people who reside in these neighbourhoods are actively engaged in determining the needs of the neighbourhoods for assistance under the legislation. I think we can be proud of these achievements, and I am delighted with the support that we have had from the provinces and municipalities. Indeed, the hon. member himself supported my predecessor in many of these programs. As we move into 1975 I am sure this program will begin to show very positive results.
Adjournment Debate
We must not overlook that it was this House that passed the legislation that required municipalities to adopt bylaws of minimum maintenance and occupancy standards. All the municipalities participating in the program have enacted these bylaws and this in itself is a most important achievement. I think the hon. member would agree, since I know he expressed concern about this when the legislation went through the House.
Turning next to implementation, the legislation prescribes that grants and loans for the rehabilitation of substandard property can be made available in NIP areas. Now that we have 33 areas designated under the NIP program it is possible for CMHC to apply the benefits of RRAP-the residential rehabilitation assistance program-and I am very happy to be able to inform the House that rehabilitation loans and grants have been made in 15 municipalities, and that many more municipalities will shortly benefit from this program.
I am the new Minister of Urban Affairs, as all hon. members know, and it would be inappropriate for me to take any credit that more properly belongs to my predecessor, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford), as well as to the provinces and municipalities which have so wholeheartedly co-operated with us in these programs. It is a co-operative effort right down the line.
It has been suggested that the rural and native housing program announced earlier this year by the federal government has been slow in getting started.

SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED INCREASES IN FAMILY ALLOWANCES AND OLD AGE PENSIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, October 2, as recorded in Hansard at page 34, I put this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde):
In view of the recommendation made to the government a few days ago by the Chairman of the Food Prices Review Board to the effect that because of drastic increases in the cost of food there should be immediate increases in family allowances and in old age security, is the government giving consideration to this recommendation?
The reply of the minister was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is surely aware that old age security pensions will be raised during October and that family allowances will also be increased as of next January 1, so as to compensate for the rise in the cost of living.
I came back with a supplementary question which was in fact an attempt on my part to say to the minister that he should have known better than to try to get away with that answer. What I was drawing to the attention of the government was the need for something more than quarterly escalation so far as old age security is concerned, and the need for something more than annual escalation so far as family allowances are concerned.
Indeed, had I time I could use a number of quotations to cite as my chief witness the Minister of National Health and Welfare himself. I shall limit myself to two or three things he said when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on Tuesday, March 13, 1973.

October 7, 1974
Adjournment Debate
At page 1:12 of the report for that day there is an indication of a discussion about the escalation of old age security. The request was being made by Liberal members that the then annual escalation be put on a quarterly basis, and this was the reply of the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
Of course it would be possible to have it twice a year. Theoretically it would even be possible to have it every three months. But every time you do that you increase your cost of administration; we have calculated that it would add about $2 million to the cost. And the money that you add to the cost of administration would not go to the senior citizens. So my inclination at the present time is to try to increase more often the total amount of benefits, including escalation, rather than load the system with more frequent escalation-
Over at page 1:22 of the same day's record the minister is reported as having said:
My point is that one way for Parliament to compensate for this unavoidable lag is to change the basic amount, every once in a while, as has been done at different times, and people catch up then-more than catch up-on what they might have lost in terms of the delays in the escalation. That is what I meant.
That was the point I was trying to make to the Minister of National Health and Welfare the other day. Escalation on the basis of the consumer price index, in which there is always a lag, never enables pensioners or recipients of family allowances to catch up with the cost of living, let alone with any rise in the standard of living.
The minister has enunciated the proposition that every once in a while there has to be an increase in the basic amount. I believe that is what Mrs. Plumptre was calling for, and that is what I am calling for now. I insist that the time has come for the government to quit relying on the quarterly escalation answer every time the plight of pensioners is raised. The time has come for an increase in the basic amount. On this first occasion of a late show in this session I want to establish this point and make it clear that this is a point I shall keep pressing until we win it.
I appreciate the fact that the minister is not able to be here tonight to answer my question, but he is well represented by a new member in the person of the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell), who comes into this House as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and will shortly be making her maiden speech. For once that phrase seems to apply, does it not?
I welcome the hon. lady particularly because she comes as the representative of a constituency that includes the area of Barrington Township, into which my ancestors moved over 200 years ago. I still regard that area as my ancestral home. I am very partial to that part of Nova Scotia and I know the kind of people the hon. lady represents.
I hope that in her initial statement tonight she will recognize the point that I am trying to make and that she will speak for her pensioners as others of us are trying to speak for the pensioners across Canada when we say that although we have welcomed quarterly escalation, if that is all we get we might as well not have secured it. What is necessary now is an increase in the basic amount of old age security and an increase in the basic amount of family allowances, and I hope that the hon. lady will be able to tell us tonight that this basic problem is under consideration.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED INCREASES IN FAMILY ALLOWANCES AND OLD AGE PENSIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
May I first congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your appointment and wish you success in the future. I must confess that I feel a certain honour that, not only as a new parliamentary secretary but also a new member of parliament, I have the pleasure of replying for the first time to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a member whose skill as a great parliamentarian is well known.
However, to get down to the specifics of the hon. member's question, since he is referring to the recommendation of the Food Prices Review Board I would draw his attention to the following quotation from page 2 of the report of the board, which reads as follows:
In the first half of 1974, after tax income in Canada rose rapidly over the corresponding level in 1973. With the exception of farm income, the main components of personal income have displayed more rapid rates of increase this year than in either of the two previous years. Transfer payments from government, reflecting particularly the substantial boost in family allowances, have played an important role in the increases in personal income this year although gains in labour income and in unincorporated business income have been building up as well.
Although I need not remind the hon. member of certain facts, I would point out to other new members like myself that family allowances were increased effective last January 1974 from an average of approximately $7 to an average of $20 per child. This amount will again be increased in January 1975 by an amount proportionate to the change in the consumer price index. I would also point out that the old age pension is being increased every three months to take into account increases in the cost of living. At present, a Canadian citizen of 65 and over is in effect guaranteed an income of not less than $199 a month.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED INCREASES IN FAMILY ALLOWANCES AND OLD AGE PENSIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: And ten cents.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED INCREASES IN FAMILY ALLOWANCES AND OLD AGE PENSIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
All this talk of personal income and after tax income may lead the hon. member to think that I am too buried in statistics to be aware of the poverty in which many of our families and senior citizens in my own area and elsewhere in Canada find themselves today. Quite the contrary. In my experience as a legal aid lawyer I have seen firsthand many of the problems they face daily. But I disagree with the hon. member when he says that a blanket increase in family allowances and old age pensions is the way to really help them at this time.
This government is presently engaged in a review of the entire social security system. As an interim step in this review the government has committed itself in the Speech from the Throne to providing allowances on an income tested basis to spouses aged 60 to 65 of old age security recipients. The speech also stated that:
The federal-provincial social security review is continuing on an urgent basis. Studies on alternative approaches to the reform of the income security system are expected to be sufficiently advanced to enable federal and provincial ministers to agree upon a preferred approach at an early date. Similarly, it is anticipated that proposals for the reform of social services will have been agreed upon shortly.

AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked to take part in the adjournment debate this evening because the matter of the sugar beet industry in western Ontario relates like a fairy tale, with the author being the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
On October 4 I asked the minister first if he would present his long awaited national sugar policy and, second, if he would indicate what progress he has made toward fulfilling his commitment to re-establish the sugar beet industry in southwestern Ontario. The minister's response can be found on page 124 of Hansard for that date. Suffice it to say we still await a national sugar policy, and the question of re-establishing the sugar beet industry was evaded.
I believe it is relevant to review the drama of the sugar beet story which has created uncertainty and frustration among a large segment of the farm community. I find it inexcusable that a large number of farmers genuinely concerned in revitalizing the sugar beet industry are but pawns in a game of politics.
Let me briefly review the story. In 1968, after an intensive investigation of the technical, social and economic aspects of the sugar beet industry, the government embarked on a program of lower trade barriers to cane sugar and the maintenance of low sugar beet production in Canada.
Let me remind you that the government of that day was the Liberal party and the policy of that day was supported by the Minister of Agriculture. As a result of that decision the last time beets were grown for the C. & D. sugar refinery in Chatham was in 1968.
The dust had barely settled when the Liberal Party had incorporated, as part of a local agricultural policy, the re-establishment of the sugar beet industry in southwestern Ontario. In the election of 1972 we had the unique situation of a sugar policy in Ottawa calling for a reduction in sugar beet production and a policy in southwestern Ontario calling for an increase in sugar beet production and a refinery.
What has happened since the election of 1972? During the last parliament the minister spoke in Chatham in January, 1973, and again in Tilbury during the month of February. On both occasions he pressed the point about establishing a sugar beet industry. Let me quote here from the London Free Press of February 24, 1973, when the minister said:
"I want a solid brief from those farmers to show that there is genuine interest in setting up a sugar beet industry here in Ontario. The next step will be to convince interested companies to set up a plant to handle the crop. If it can be shown farmers are willing to produce a large enough crop to allow for economic operation year in, year out, I think they will put up the refinery."
Adjournment Debate
"That's what I mean when I say that I want a national sugar policy. There's a heck of a lot of work still to do, but I think we can do it, and I think we can get a new industry for our farmers."
Mr. Speaker, let me remind you that during that same period of time, the two policy era, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) had introduced a budget in which he proposed a tariff reduction of 30 cents per 100 pounds of imported raw sugar, clearly supporting the position of 1968.
Again on December 17, 1973, as recorded at page 8795 of Hansard the following exchange took place:
Me. James A. McGrath (St. John's East): Mr. Speaker, I ask the Minister of Agriculture, by way of a supplementary question, whether, in view of the very serious situation regarding the sugar market and the effect this will have on the cost of living in Canada, he is now prepared, after two years, to bring in his sugar policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my sugar policy is not two years delayed; and by the time the two years are up you can be sure we will have a new sugar beet industry and a new sugar refining industry in western Ontario and a policy for all of Canada.
I specifically asked my question last Friday because this matter was shelved during the recent election campaign and frankly, sir, the minister's response has not been reassuring.
I should like to quote from the "Lambton Farmer" of February 14, 1973. There is an article entitled "Can Beets Come Back? Some Say It's Wrong," which reports an interview with Professor Donald Thain of the School of Business, University of Western Ontario. He was a member of the federal task force which produced the book "Canadian Agriculture in the Seventies". The article quotes Professor Thain as follows:
"I'm certain this is happening now because the Liberals are in a vulnerable position," said the western professor. "They need votes. This couldn't have happened two or three years ago because they didn't have to be concerned then about buying votes with sugar beets."
I am not going to accuse the minister of such tactics. I am a reasonable man and I am prepared to accept his promises as genuine and sincere. However, I believe that time is running out. I believe the minister is responsible for presenting a national sugar policy to parliament. Sir, he made a commitment to establish a sugar beet industry in southwestern Ontario, an industry which he said earlier would be in operation by the end of 1974. In conclusion I simply ask the minister either for honesty or for action.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join my colleagues in congratulating you on the position you have been called to hold.
The hon. member asked two questions: 1-Whether the Minister of Agriculture could advise the House of his national policy on sugar, and 2-What progress has been made with regard to his commitment to restore the beet industry in south western Ontario.
In his reply, the minister mentioned some of the problems that will have to be studied, adding that his department is working on them and that he will submit a report to his colleagues as soon as possible.
28305-14"/:

October 7, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Amongst the problems mentioned by the Food Prices Review Board is that of production, total demand and the increase in the cost of production.
Some of these problems are the competition of other crops in sugar beet and sugar cane producing countries, a change in the membership of the European Economic Community, amendments to the international agreement on sugar and the challenge in the United States Congress of the American agreement on sugar.
The government has already made changes to the sugar rate structure, but when considering new changes, we must give our approval to some countries like Australia.
The Minister of Agriculture still believes that sugar beets can be grown in Ontario, and as in other parts of the world there is strong competition, on a cost-benefit basis, from other products such as wheat and soybeans.
All these crops vie for available lands. Even in western Canada, there exists sugar beet refineries.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the hon. member that it is an important issue and as the minister said in his answer, he hopes to produce a report once his colleagues have considered his suggestions.
